<reason>Both sides built coherent, well-grounded cases, but A executed the rebuttal chain more decisively. A's pressure question exposed that B's "consent" standard had no defined threshold, and B's answer ("a test of alternatives... a pilot tied to visible gains earns acquiescence") never supplied one — a real gap A exploited cleanly in closing ("veto with a review date attached"). A also neutralized B's captivity/regressivity dichotomy attempt reasonably well once B clarified it (different drivers, not the same trip), and answered B's cliff-exemption pressure with a genuinely responsive mechanism (flat per-capita rebate) that removed the means-testing problem B had raised. B's strongest counter — that a flat rebate still leaves high-frequency low-income drivers net worse off while low-driving elites profit — was a real and undamaged point, but A's closing simply reasserted the funding logic without conceding or refining, and B's own closing likewise never advanced past repeating this point, so it stayed unresolved rather than decisively winning the round for B. A's structural advantage (funding can't precede pricing; unbounded "consent" is functionally unfalsifiable) proved more damaging to B's live route than B's regressivity critique was to A's. A's opening being clipped for length is a genuine execution cost, but it did not remove core arguments that were echoed later, so it only marginally tempers an otherwise cleaner performance.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Q2 pressure question forcing B to define a concrete threshold for acceptable opposition, and B's vague non-answer ("a test of alternatives... earns acquiescence"), which A then converted into the closing's most memorable line: "veto with a review date attached."</best_rebuttal>
